about: Texts read from outside this house for this work. No source document is committed; build.py fetches each, asserts the PDF's hash, and finds each passage (in the 1977 scan by its letters, since the scan is two columns read through OCR; in the abstracts and the Unicode annex word for word).

sources.cite: Richard E. Nisbett and Timothy DeCamp Wilson, 'Telling More Than We Can Know: Verbal Reports on Mental Processes', Psychological Review 84 (3), 1977, 231–259. doi:10.1037/0033-295X.84.3.231
sources.read: 2026-11-19, in full, as this cycle's reach outside (experimental social psychology, a field this practice had not used). The university's own repository (hdl:2027.42/92167) served a page instead of the file; this copy is a scan of the journal pages.

passages.text: if the reports of subjects do not differ from the reports of observers, then it is unnecessary to assume that the former are drawing on "a fount of privileged knowledge"

passages.text: It seems equally clear that subjects and observers are drawing on a similar source for their verbal reports about stimulus effects.
The only mystery is why people are so poor at telling the difference between private facts that can be known with near certainty and mental processes to which there may be no access at all.
passages.where: section 'Why are we unaware of our unawareness?'

passages.text: Kit Fine (1975) assigned truth-values top-down by counting a statement as true if it comes out true under all admissible precisifications of the entire language
the method of supervaluations allows one to retain all the theorems of standard logic while admitting “truth-value gaps”

sources.cite: Kit Fine, 'Vagueness, Truth and Logic', Synthese 30 (3/4), 1975, 265–300. doi:10.1007/BF00485047
sources.read: 2026-11-21, in full, by the check (state 3): the critique of state 2 named it unread. The host refuses a scripted fetch (a browser challenge, and through a real browser 'upstream request failed'), so the paper was read through a page-extraction service from that copy, a scan of the journal pages (JSTOR stable 20115033). The extracted text is not committed; its sha256 as read is recorded. build3.py --fine <text> finds every passage again in a copy anyone obtains.

passages.text: Very roughly, vagueness is deficiency of meaning. As such, it is to be distinguished from generality, undecidability, and ambiguity.
nice2 is ambiguous, its meaning is over-determined
passages.where: p. 266 (the scan prints the subscript as a digit)

passages.text: a vague sentence is true if true for all complete precisifications ; an ambiguous sentence is true if true for all disambiguations.
to assert an ambiguous sentence is to assert, severally
passages.where: p. 282 (followed by the mark of note 9)

passages.text: precisifications are extended from a common basis and according to common constraints
biguity is like the super-imposition of several pictures, vagueness like an unfinished picture, with marginal notes for completion.

sources.cite: Marc Brysbaert, 'How many words do we read per minute? A review and meta-analysis of reading rate', Journal of Memory and Language 109 (2019) 104047. doi:10.1016/j.jml.2019.104047
sources.read: 2026-11-21, the abstract and the sections on the 300-word norm, for the rates of the two-minute rule (state 3). A copy of the published article.

passages.text: we estimate that the average silent reading rate for adults in English is 238 words per minute (wpm) for non-fiction and 260 wpm for fiction
The average oral reading rate (based on 77 studies and 5965 participants) is 183 wpm.
Reading rates are lower for children, old adults, and readers with English as second language.
For silent reading of English non-fiction most adults fall in the range of 175–300 wpm
